title: Calibration without labels in multiple testing
claim: A calibration-aware estimator's regret shrinks steadily with sample size, while raw and standard error measures plateau at a miscalibration floor.
layout: 3x3 grid of log-log line plots, shared axes, one legend on top
description: A 3x3 grid of log-log line plots. Each panel is titled with a simulation scenario: rows set the null proportion π0 (0.5, 0.75, 0.9) and columns set the alternative-density parameter α (0.5, 0.95, 1.5). The x-axis is sample size, from about 10^3 to 10^5. The y-axis is expected Brier regret, from about 10^-3 to 10^-1. A legend across the top names three methods: red circles for q-value, yellow squares for p-value, and blue triangles for the isotonic lfdr estimator. In nearly every panel the yellow and red curves are nearly flat, so their regret does not improve with more data. The blue curve slopes steadily downward, which shows consistent convergence. The blue curve is clearly lowest in most panels. The exception is the top-right panels, where the curves start close together and cross. The eye goes first to the falling blue lines.
caption: $\log$-$\log$ plots for simulation studies of (inductive) expected Brier regret for $p$-values, $q$-values and the isotonic calibration estimator $\widehat\lfdr_\uparrow$. Each panel represents a new simulation scenario, with different null proportion $\pinull$ and parameter $\alpha$ for the alternative density.
abstract: Large-scale hypothesis testing supports probability claims about individual hypotheses, as in empirical Bayes methods for estimating local false discovery rates. We study how such claims can be interpreted as approximately calibrated forecasts of the null hypothesis, yielding interpretable error probabilities even under model misspecification. Our approach draws conceptual inspiration from probabilistic forecasting but addresses a different challenge: unlike forecasting, where labels are eventually observed, in multiple testing the ground truth is never revealed, so calibration must be assessed stochastically and established indirectly. We address this challenge by constructing a set of pseudo-labels, derived from the spacings of ordered $p$-values, which have the local false discovery rate as their regression target. Our construction unlocks existing tools for assessing and performing post-hoc calibration in multiple testing. Notably, we find on a large-scale empirical survey of published psychology and neuroscience literature that the $q$-value, a popular error measure based on the false discovery rate, can be severely miscalibrated.
